title: Heap, Intervals & Greedy
html:
Heap, Intervals & Greedy

Three topics that keep appearing together, because interval problems are usually solved by sorting and then either a heap or a greedy sweep.

Heaps

A complete binary tree where every parent beats its children, stored in a plain array. Peek O(1), push and pop O(log n), and building from n items in O(n) rather than O(n log n) by sifting down from the middle.

It is only partially ordered - the second smallest could be either child of the root. That weaker guarantee is precisely why it is cheaper than a sorted structure, and why iterating a heap does not give sorted output.

Where it fits:

  • Top k. Keep a heap of size k. O(n log k), and O(k) space - which matters when n does not fit in memory.
  • Streaming. Two heaps, a max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper, keep the running median.
  • Repeated "cheapest next". Merging k sorted sources; Dijkstra's frontier.

Intervals

Nearly every interval problem starts with a sort, and what you sort by determines the algorithm:

  • Sort by start - merging overlaps. Walk through, extending the current interval while the next one starts before the current ends.
  • Sort by end - maximum non-overlapping count. Always take the earliest-ending compatible interval; it leaves the most room.
  • Sort by start, heap of ends - minimum rooms or machines. Pop every meeting that has finished before the next begins; the heap's peak size is the answer.

Sweep line is the alternative: turn each interval into a +1 at its start and a −1 at its end, sort the events, and run a counter. The running total is the number of overlaps at that point, and its maximum is the peak. Handles "how many at once" more directly than pairwise comparison.

The edge case to settle before writing anything: does [1,2] overlap [2,3]? Half-open intervals [start, end) make this unambiguous and are almost always the right choice.

Greedy

Take the locally best option and never reconsider. When it works it is simpler and faster than DP; when it does not, it produces a plausible wrong answer, which is worse than failing.

Greedy is correct when the problem has the greedy-choice property: a locally optimal choice is part of some globally optimal solution. That needs an argument, not a hunch. The usual one is an exchange argument - show that any optimal solution can be rewritten to include your choice without getting worse.

Where it holds: interval scheduling by earliest end; Huffman coding; minimum spanning trees; coin change for canonical coin systems.

Where it fails: coin change in general. With coins 1, 3, 4 and a target of 6, greedy takes 4 then 1 then 1 - three coins - where 3 + 3 is two. Nothing in the greedy run signals the mistake.

The practical test: if you cannot articulate why the local choice is safe, assume it is not and reach for DP.

Common mistakes

  • Sorting by the wrong key, which silently changes the problem being solved.
  • Leaving interval boundary inclusivity undecided until a test fails.
  • Using a min-heap where the largest is wanted, or negating values and forgetting to negate back.
  • Asserting a greedy choice is optimal without an exchange argument.
